Abrar F.lab_name: NeurdyPhagy Lab, Department of Biology, University of Waterloo (Waterloo, Ontario, Canada)
Abrar F.role: First author of a 2026 review on how chemical tags on the autophagy receptor SQSTM1/p62 are linked to neurodegenerative disease
Abrar F.sub: Department of Biology, University of Waterloo · NeurdyPhagy Lab (M.Sc. student, according to the lab's people page)
story: Fatima Abrar is the first author of a 2026 review in Autophagy, written with Dale D. O. Martin. The review is about SQSTM1/p62, a protein that grabs damaged or unwanted cell material and hands it to the autophagy system, the cell's recycling pathway. The authors go through the small chemical tags added to p62 after it is made (phosphorylation, ubiquitination, acetylation, S-acylation and S-nitrosylation) and show how each tag changes where p62 sits and what it does. This matters for diseases such as Alzheimer disease, ALS and Huntington disease, where this tidying system goes wrong. It is a review of published work, not a new experiment, and mTORC1, the growth-control complex, is one of the regulators it covers.

Abrar works in the NeurdyPhagy Lab, led by Dale Martin at the University of Waterloo Department of Biology. The lab's people page lists Abrar as a Master's student and says the research looks at how protein mislocalization affects proteins needed for autophagy in Huntington disease. PubMed shows Abrar as first author of a 2025 research paper in the FASEB Journal on reduced palmitoylation of p62 in Huntington disease, and as co-author of a 2024 paper on the protein SVIP and a 2023 review on palmitoylation in neurodegeneration, all from the same lab. A current position beyond the lab page could not be confirmed.

highlights.ABR2026: First author of the review, one of two authors, working in the Department of Biology at the University of Waterloo.

Stracka D.role: Co-author of two studies from Michael Hall's laboratory in Basel that placed mTORC2, the second mTOR complex, at the ribosome and at contact sites between the endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria
Stracka D.sub: Biozentrum, University of Basel (Hall laboratory, papers 2011–2015)
story: Daniele Stracka is second author on two Atlas studies from Michael Hall's group at the Biozentrum in Basel. The 2011 paper in Cell (ZIN2011) showed that mTORC2, the rapamycin-insensitive mTOR complex, is switched on when it binds the ribosome, the cell's protein factory, downstream of the growth signal PI3K. The 2013 paper in PNAS (BET2013) found that mTORC2 and its target Akt also sit at mitochondria-associated membranes, the contact points between the endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria, where they help control how mitochondria work. Both studies are experiments in cells.

PubMed lists four papers under this name, all from the Biozentrum in Basel and all with the given name Daniele. The two Atlas studies themselves give no affiliation for him. The Basel link comes from the two other papers, so the evidence for the identity rests on the rare surname, the same given name and the same laboratory head in all four. No official page or current position was found.

highlights.ZIN2011: Second author of the paper showing that mTORC2 is activated by association with the ribosome.
highlights.BET2013: Second author of the paper placing mTORC2-Akt signalling at mitochondria-associated ER membranes.

Lin S.role: Co-author of the 2008 mouse study showing that muscle needs raptor, the mTORC1 component, to stay healthy
story: Shuo Lin is the fourth of thirteen authors on a 2008 study in Cell Metabolism from the Biozentrum in Basel. The team removed raptor, a key part of the growth-control complex mTORC1, only in the skeletal muscle of mice. These muscles slowly became dystrophic and the mice did not live long. Removing rictor, the matching part of mTORC2, had no such effect. The work was done in mice, so it shows what mTORC1 does in mouse muscle, not directly in people.

PubMed does not list an affiliation for Shuo Lin in this 2008 record. The Biozentrum, University of Basel link comes from a 2013 muscle paper on mTORC1 in atrophy and hypertrophy, where Shuo Lin appears next to the same group members (Bentzinger, Romanino, Hall and Rüegg), and a 2019 raptor paper from the same institute. The Atlas does not carry a source for the person's role, training or current position.

highlights.BEN2008: Fourth of thirteen authors on the paper that deleted raptor or rictor in mouse skeletal muscle.

Chen WW.lab_name: Department of Pediatrics, UT Southwestern Medical Center (Dallas, Texas, USA)
Chen WW.role: Co-author of the 2017 Cell paper showing that SLC38A9 releases essential amino acids from lysosomes to switch on mTORC1
Chen WW.sub: Instructor, Department of Pediatrics, UT Southwestern Medical Center · Fellowship in Neonatal-Perinatal Medicine, UT Southwestern (2024) · Pediatrics residency, Boston Children's Hospital (2021) · Harvard Medical School M.D.-Ph.D. Program · Whitehead Institute and MIT (2017)
story: The Atlas study from 2017 asked what the lysosome, the cell's recycling compartment, does for mTORC1, the growth-control complex. The authors showed that a lysosomal membrane protein called SLC38A9 senses the amino acid arginine and pushes essential amino acids such as leucine out of the lysosome. That leucine then helps switch mTORC1 on. The work used human cells and mice, and pancreatic cancer cells that live on protein they take in from outside needed SLC38A9 to form tumors.

Walter W. Chen is a middle author on this paper. PubMed lists him at the Whitehead Institute, MIT, the Koch Institute and the Broad Institute in Cambridge, and in the Harvard Medical School M.D.-Ph.D. Program. A Whitehead news item describes him as a graduate student in David Sabatini's lab who later became a pediatrics resident, and a UT Southwestern page lists a PhD from MIT in 2016, Harvard Medical School in 2018, pediatrics residency at Boston Children's Hospital in 2021 and a neonatal-perinatal fellowship at UT Southwestern in 2024. The same page gives his current title as Instructor in Pediatrics. His PubMed record also shows several other papers from the Sabatini group on cancer and mitochondrial metabolism.

highlights.WYA2017: Middle author of the SLC38A9 paper, listed at the Whitehead Institute and the Harvard Medical School M.D.-Ph.D. Program.

Rüegg MA.role: Neurobiologist at the Biozentrum of the University of Basel who studies how muscles and the nerve connections that drive them develop, age and fail, and a co-author on three early mouse and cell studies that mapped what mTORC1 and mTORC2 do in muscle, fat and liver
Rüegg MA.sub: Professor of Neurobiology, Biozentrum, University of Basel · Co-founder and CEO, SEAL Therapeutics (since 2021) · Postdoctoral fellow, Stanford University (1989–1992)
story: Markus Rüegg is a middle author on three Atlas studies from the Biozentrum in Basel, all done together with Michael Hall's group. In 2004, the group showed in mouse cells that a second mTOR complex, mTORC2, exists. It is not blocked by rapamycin and helps control the actin cytoskeleton, the protein scaffold that gives a cell its shape. In 2008, mice that lacked raptor, a key part of mTORC1, only in fat tissue stayed lean and burned more energy in their mitochondria. In 2012, mice that lacked rictor, a key part of mTORC2, only in the liver could not switch the liver from making glucose to using it after a meal, and they developed high blood sugar and low blood fats.

The Biozentrum website lists Rüegg as full professor of neurobiology at the University of Basel since 2004, after earlier posts there as assistant and associate professor. He studied biochemistry at the University of Zurich and worked as a postdoctoral fellow in the neurobiology department at Stanford University School of Medicine from 1989 to 1992. His group studies how the junction between nerve and muscle is built and kept up, muscle ageing and muscular dystrophies. The same group showed in 2008 that muscle without raptor becomes dystrophic, which is how mTORC1 entered his muscle work. Since 2021 he has also been co-founder and CEO of SEAL Therapeutics. His part in the Atlas studies is as a co-author, and the Atlas findings come from mice and cultured cells, not from people.

highlights.JAC2004: Middle author of the paper that described mTORC2 in mammalian cells, together with Michael Hall and colleagues at the Biozentrum.
highlights.POL2008: Middle author of the paper showing that removing raptor from fat tissue makes mice lean.
highlights.HAG2012: Middle author of the paper showing that liver-specific loss of rictor disturbs how the liver handles glucose and fat.

Guibaud L.lab_name: Pediatric and Fetal Imaging, Reference Center for Superficial Vascular Anomalies, Hôpital Femme Mère Enfant, Université Claude Bernard Lyon 1 (Lyon, France)
Guibaud L.role: First author of a 2026 case series on giving sirolimus (rapamycin) to pregnant women to treat large lymphatic malformations in their unborn babies
Guibaud L.sub: Pediatric and Fetal Imaging, Hôpital Femme Mère Enfant, Université Claude Bernard Lyon 1 (Lyon-Bron) · INSERM U1151, Necker Enfants Malades Institute (Paris)
story: Lymphatic malformations are clusters of abnormal fluid-filled channels that can grow large before birth. When they press on a baby's airway, breathing at birth can be dangerous. Sirolimus (rapamycin) blocks mTOR, the cell growth switch, and is used after birth for such lesions. This paper asks whether the mother can take it during pregnancy. In six pregnancies, treatment started between 24 and over 30 weeks, maternal side effects were mild, and the drug crossed the placenta. Five of the six newborns showed partial or marked shrinkage of the lesion on imaging. It was a small observational series, so it cannot show that the drug caused the improvement.

Laurent Guibaud is first author. PubMed lists him in the pediatric and fetal imaging unit of the Hôpital Femme Mère Enfant in Lyon-Bron, which is a reference center for superficial vascular anomalies, and at the Necker Enfants Malades Institute in Paris. His identity was checked through a related 2026 paper in Prenatal Diagnosis on maternal sirolimus for a fetal vascular tumor, which lists Laurent Guibaud at the same Lyon center and shares several co-authors with this series, among them Guillaume Canaud, Alexandre Guilhem, Sara Cabet and Antoine Fraissenon. A 2026 imaging review of venous malformations also lists him in the same unit.

highlights.GUIB2026: First author and lead of the Lyon imaging team that described patient selection, sirolimus management and outcomes in six pregnancies.
